results.name: item_level_rating_variance
results.description: Variance across (set, target) items of the item mean yes rate; observed above null means people's judgments are more sharply all-or-none across items than the model's graded similarity predicts (model too flat), below means the model over-discriminates.

results.name: rule_consistent_minus_inconsistent
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share at least one arithmetic property (even/odd, mult of 3/4/5/10, same final digit, prime, square, power of 2), yes rate for targets having ALL shared properties minus yes rate for targets lacking any; observed above null means people apply the shared rule more sharply than graded summed similarity predicts.

results.name: singleton_minus_multi_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on 1-example sets minus yes rate on sets with 2-4 examples; summed similarity predicts more examples -> more yes (negative value), so an observed value above the null means the model under-produces generalization from single examples relative to multi-example sets (no size-principle tightening).

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets more than 25 away from every example (magnitude-distant targets); observed above null means the model under-predicts acceptance of numerically distant targets (people generalize by rule, not by magnitude proximity), below means it over-predicts.
results.code:
# name: far_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets more than 25 away from every example (magnitude-distant targets); observed above null means the model under-predicts acceptance of numerically distant targets (people generalize by rule, not by magnitude proximity), below means it over-predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()[:, None]
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(s - t), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = d > 25
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: trial_index_yes_slope
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the yes response; the model has no time dependence (null near 0), so an observed positive value means people drift toward saying yes more later in the session, which the model fails to produce.

results.name: singleton_distance_correlation
results.description: For 1-example sets only, Pearson correlation between yes response and |target - example|; strongly negative means magnitude-driven generalization, so an observed value above (closer to 0 than) the null means the model over-weights numeric proximity for single examples, below means it under-weights it.

results.name: within_set_target_spread
results.description: Mean over sets of the std of target-level yes rates within the same set (how differently targets for one set are treated); observed above null means the model under-differentiates targets within a set (too graded), below means it over-differentiates.

results.name: inside_minus_outside_range
results.description: For sets with 2-4 examples, yes rate for targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus yes rate for targets outside that range; observed above null means people treat the span of examples as a hypothesis region more strongly than summed exemplar similarity predicts.
results.code:
# name: inside_minus_outside_range
# description: For sets with 2-4 examples, yes rate for targets inside [min,max] of the examples minus yes rate for targets outside that range; observed above null means people treat the span of examples as a hypothesis region more strongly than summed exemplar similarity predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1)
    lo = s.min(axis=1)
    hi = s.max(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    multi = n >= 2
    inside = multi & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    outside = multi & ~((t >= lo) & (t <= hi))
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())
